new_statements.quote: Die Akzentverteilung ist die in konservativen Dialekten übliche, also mit Akzent auf der letzten Wortsilbe bzw. auf den ursprünglichen Flexionsmorphemen. Eine Ausnahme ist másek 'Monat'. Entlehnte Nomina und Adjektiva sind in der Grundform nicht endbetont, wohl aber im Obliquus. Die Verben tragen den Akzent auf den Personalmorphemen, auch bei den entlehnten vom Typ har-in-áva 'sich verspäten'. Auf d auslautende Wurzeln haben den Akzent teilweise noch auf der Wurzel (vázdela), teilweise ist die Verteilung aber schon dem Gros der Verben (z.B. kandéla 'hören', khandéla 'riechen' F. nach mangéla) angeglichen worden.
new_statements.translation: The distribution of the accent is the one usual in conservative dialects, i.e. with the accent on the last syllable of the word, or rather on the original inflectional morphemes. One exception is másek 'month'. Borrowed nouns and adjectives are not end-stressed in their base form, but they are in the oblique. Verbs carry the accent on the person morphemes, also in borrowed ones of the type har-in-áva 'to be late'. Roots ending in d partly still have the accent on the root (vázdela), but partly the distribution has already been levelled to the bulk of the verbs (e.g. kandéla 'hear', khandéla 'smell' F., after mangéla).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Conservative Romani pattern: stress on the last syllable of the word, more precisely on the original (Layer I) inflectional morphemes: native nouns/adjectives are oxytonic, verbs stress the person ending (mangéla), and the agglutinated Layer II case suffixes stay unstressed (so in oblique forms the stress is on the old ending, not the absolute last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: másek 'month' (non-final); borrowed nouns and adjectives keep non-final stress in the base form but are end-stressed in the oblique; a few d-final verb roots keep root stress (vázdela), others have levelled to ending stress (kandéla, khandéla)
new_statements.identity_note: Boretzky 1996 describes Arli of Macedonia and Kosovo (informants from Skopje, Prilep, Gilan/Gnjilane and the Prizren area; sigla Ba., P., Gi., F., I.), which is within balk1252 (arli1238). Friedman 2000 speaks of Balkan Romani dialects as a group with Macedonia singled out; Kostov 1996 speaks of 'Balkan-Romani' loanwords. Matras 2002 is a survey of Romani as a whole, not specific to balk1252.

new_statements.quote: An interesting feature of Romani prosody is the fact that stress placement remains quite conservative in the Balkans, whereas elsewhere there is a tendency to adapt to the stress of the major contact language. Thus most Balkan Romani dialects have oxytonic stress in native words, non-oxytonic in foreign words. This is especially striking in Macedonia, where the general tendency is to shift the stress away from the final syllable.

new_statements.quote: 4.2.6 Stress Early Romani had word-level grammatical stress, which is preserved in con- temporary Romani in what Boretzky and Igla (1993) call ‘conservative’ stress petterns [sic scanned]. In the pre-European (‘thematic’) component, stress is on the final position of lexical roots, in the absence of grammatical affixes, or on older [...] [p. 64:] patterns of Albanian, which often result in penultimate stress. The affected dialects include varieties of Bugurdzi, Arli, and others. In both groups, the process still [...] ongoing and stress is subject to variation. Consistent shifts are reported for the Terzi Mahale dialect of Prizren (penultimate) and for Finnish Romani (initial).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Matras describes the inherited (Early Romani) system as word-level GRAMMATICAL stress, preserved in 'conservative' dialects (Boretzky & Igla's term): in pre-European (thematic) vocabulary stress falls on the last syllable of the lexical root when no grammatical affix follows, otherwise on the older (Layer I) inflectional endings of nouns, pronouns, possessives, adjectives and on person inflection of verbs (mediopassives keep root stress); a following ending 'carries the stress (in dialects with conservative stress patterns)'. For the Balkan varieties of this glottocode he then reports a contact-induced drift AWAY from that system: under Albanian(-type) stress patterns there is a shift that 'often result[s] in penultimate stress'; 'the affected dialects include varieties of Bugurdži, Arli, and others', where 'the process [is] still ongoing and stress is subject to variation', while a CONSISTENT penultimate shift is reported for the Terzi Mahale dialect of Prizren.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the visible fragments
new_statements.exceptions: (i) loan (athematic) vocabulary is outside the conservative final/affix-stress rule ('Full assimilation of athematic..' fragment; details not visible); (ii) penultimate shift ongoing with variation in varieties of Bugurdži and Arli; (iii) consistent penultimate stress in Terzi Mahale (Prizren); (iv) elsewhere in the section: Finnish Romani initial, some Central dialects initial, Eastern Slovak and Sinti keep grammatical stress on Layer I endings (roméskero exempt from the penult shift).
new_statements.identity_note: Matras 2002 is a pan-Romani handbook; the quoted p. 64 sentences name exactly the three varieties of this glottocode's label: Bugurdži, Arli (varieties of; Macedonia/Kosovo/Serbia) and the Terzi Mahale dialect of Prizren (Kosovo). The general pp. 62-63 statement is about Early Romani / conservative dialects as a class (Boretzky & Igla's 'conservative stress'), not about one variety.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction. The catalog (Boretzky & Igla 1994), Boretzky 1996 (Arli) and Friedman 2000 all code these Balkan varieties as conservative: stress on the final syllable of inherited words = on the old inflectional morphemes, loans non-final. Matras 2002 (as far as the open scanned fragments of 4.2.6 show) states the same conservative grammatical-stress baseline, citing Boretzky & Igla, but adds a qualification the catalog record does not carry: varieties of Bugurdži and Arli are 'affected dialects' of an ongoing, variable shift toward penultimate stress under Albanian-type contact, and the Terzi Mahale dialect of Prizren shows a CONSISTENT penultimate shift (p. 64). For the Prizren member of this glottocode that is a different placement (penultimate) from the final/morphological one implied by the single catalog record; Boretzky & Igla themselves note the conservative type is seen 'sehr schlecht im Bug[urdži]'. The two [..] gaps in the fragments (what the 'second centre' sentence says before 'patterns of Albanian', and the continuation of 'or on older..') could not be filled because archive.org was unreachable (probe failed) and Google Books could not be reached by automated download.

Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/9781139019095.007 (Open Access, CC-BY 4.0). §5.5 Prosody, pp. 460ff; §5.5.1 Prosodic Loss pp. 461-463; §5.5.2 Accentual realization pp. 463-470.

tone.quote: Still, the basic observation is that there have been changes in the prosodic systems of several of the Balkan languages, and while some of them might have been independent of one another, it is undeniable that there is a regional clustering of loss of both length and tone in the Balkans and the fixing of stress no further back than the antepenult (with minor exceptions) as opposed to length and freer or even fixed initial stress north of the peninsula. The loss of Latin length in Balkan Romance and also of Albanian length in much of Tosk can also be mentioned here. In the case of Romani, Indic length was lost before arrival in the Balkans, but Romani north of the Balkans in contact with languages with distinctive length have developed new length as a result of contact (Matras 2002: 59–60).
tone.locator: §5.5.1 Prosodic Loss, pp. 462-463; stress rule §5.5.2 p. 470
